title: Line endings and .gitattributes
summary: Why a script fails with bad interpreter after a Windows commit, why a pull request shows every line changed, and the two-line fix the whole team shares.

steps.title: Two symptoms, one cause
body: Windows tools end lines with CR LF (`\r\n`), Linux and macOS with LF (`\n`). When the wrong ending reaches the repository:
bash: ./deploy.sh: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
(`^M` is the CR), or a pull request where someone changed one line and the diff shows **all** of them.
The fix that works for everyone is a committed `.gitattributes` at the top of the repo. It overrides each person's `core.autocrlf`:
* text=auto eol=lf      # Git decides what is text; text is stored and checked out with LF
*.ps1 text eol=crlf     # files that must stay CRLF on every machine
Adding it does not fix files already committed. `git add --renormalize .` rewrites them in the index, and `git ls-files --eol` shows what is stored (`i/lf`, `i/crlf`) and what is on disk (`w/...`).

steps.prompt: Why do teams commit `.gitattributes` instead of asking everyone to set `core.autocrlf`?
options: It travels with the repository, so every clone on every OS follows the same rules
steps.explain: `core.autocrlf` is a personal setting (the Git for Windows installer sets it to `true`), so one misconfigured laptop is enough to commit CRLF. Attributes are part of the repo and win over it.

steps.title: Fix the bad interpreter for good
prompt: In `~/ops`, `./deploy.sh prod` fails with `/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter`. Ana committed it from Windows with CRLF endings, and `app.yaml` too.
1. Prove it: `git ls-files --eol` (look for `i/crlf`) or `file deploy.sh`.
2. Add a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf`, renormalize the committed files, and commit both as `Normalize line endings to LF`.
3. Refresh your working copy so `./deploy.sh prod` prints `deploying prod`.

checks.name: the repository stores LF now
checks.cmd: cd ~/ops && git ls-files --eol deploy.sh app.yaml | grep -c 'i/lf'
checks.fail: `git ls-files --eol` should show `i/lf` for both files. `git add --renormalize .` after adding `.gitattributes`.

checks.name: .gitattributes is committed with the rule
checks.cmd: cd ~/ops && git show HEAD:.gitattributes | grep -qE '^\* +text=auto +eol=lf' && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = 'Normalize line endings to LF'
checks.fail: Commit `.gitattributes` (with `* text=auto eol=lf`) and the renormalized files as `Normalize line endings to LF`.

checks.name: the script runs
checks.fail: Your working copy still has CR characters. Remove the files and restore them from the index: `rm deploy.sh app.yaml && git restore deploy.sh app.yaml`.

hints: `git ls-files --eol` shows `i/crlf w/crlf` for the two files.
`echo '* text=auto eol=lf' > .gitattributes`, `git add .gitattributes`, `git add --renormalize .`, then commit.
The files on disk still have CRLF: `rm deploy.sh app.yaml` and `git restore deploy.sh app.yaml` writes them fresh with LF.
solution: git commit -m "Normalize line endings to LF"
steps.explain: The normalizing commit touches every line of the affected files once, so do it in its own commit and add its hash to `.git-blame-ignore-revs`. For a quick one-off on a server, `sed -i 's/\r$//' deploy.sh` (or Vim's `:set ff=unix`) fixes the file, but only `.gitattributes` stops it from coming back.

steps.prompt: Match the `.gitattributes` line to what it does.
pairs: store text with LF and check it out with LF everywhere
always check these out with CRLF
never convert or diff these bytes
shell scripts keep LF even on Windows
